verdict.justification: B is the stronger operational SOP because it gives warehouse staff clearer, more consistent instructions across receiving, storage, kitting, transport, returns, and exception handling. Its transport rule, “Do not carry loose ESDS items, even within the EPA,” avoids A’s ambiguous allowance that “open or partly filled containers need an ESD cart,” which could be read as permitting movement of exposed items outside a protected area. B also provides more actionable failure responses, including retesting failed personal grounding equipment and segregating items handled since the last passing test. Its handling instruction permits holding components by the package body or board edges, whereas A’s blanket prohibition on touching “component bodies” is unnecessarily restrictive for routine component handling. B more explicitly integrates training authorization, calibration, log review, and record ownership into daily operations. Both remain approval-stage drafts requiring technical validation, and the extracted text does not establish whether either meets the five-page limit, but B would require less procedural clarification before implementation.

decisive_issues.issue: Transport instructions leave an ambiguous route for moving exposed items rather than consistently requiring enclosure.
decisive_issues.quote: open or partly filled containers need an ESD cart

decisive_issues.issue: Blanket prohibition on touching component bodies is impractical compared with distinguishing package bodies from leads and contacts.
decisive_issues.quote: Do not touch leads, contacts or component bodies; hold items by the edges or the packaging.

decisive_issues.issue: Provides a clear containment boundary when personal grounding fails after handling.
decisive_issues.quote: Segregate items handled since the last PASS test, bag in shielding packaging, tag ‘SUSPECT – ESD’.

decisive_issues.issue: Makes equipment calibration an explicit assigned and recorded control.
